\chapter{Want, Can, Must}
\label{ch:fr-modaux}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I want, what I can do and what I must do, put any verb I already know behind vouloir, pouvoir or devoir without changing it, and choose je voudrais over je veux when I am asking rather than stating.}

Three verbs that between them open a sentence for every verb the reader already owns -- and the point at which correct French used at the wrong moment is named as a harder mistake to hear than a grammatical one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vouloir]{vouloir — to want}

\label{lesson:FR-C33-vouloir}



\begin{quote}
Put \textbf{est-ce que} in front of a statement and it becomes a question. Hold that; you will need it in a moment.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vouloir} — \textbf{to want}. Here are the singular forms, which is what you need first:

Say it as a chant, three beats:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je veux — tu veux — il veut}
\end{quote}

\emph{I want, you want, he wants.} And notice what your ear reports: \textbf{all three sound identical}. \emph{veux}, \emph{veux}, \emph{veut} — the spelling distinguishes them and the mouth does not. That is why French keeps the subject pronoun in front: without \emph{je} or \emph{tu}, nothing tells a listener who wants what.

Then a \emph{want} needs something wanted, and it follows directly:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Je veux un café.} — I want a coffee.
  \item \textbf{Tu veux le pain ?} — Do you want the bread?
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Now the part a phrasebook will not tell you, and the reason this word needs a warning where \emph{parler} did not.

\textbf{Je veux is blunt.} Said to a waiter or a shopkeeper it lands close to English \emph{I want}, which is to say it lands badly. French has a softened form built for exactly this, and it is the one you should reach for by default:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je voudrais} — \emph{I would like}
\end{quote}

Same verb, different shape. \textbf{Je voudrais un café} is what a French speaker actually says across a counter, and it is no harder to say than \emph{je veux}.

So learn both, and learn when each belongs. \emph{Je veux} is for a want you are simply stating — to a friend, to a child, about yourself. \textbf{Je voudrais is for asking anyone for anything.} If you are unsure which you are doing, you are asking, and you want \emph{voudrais}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{je veux, tu veux, il veut} — and hear that all three are the same sound
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{je voudrais un café}, as though to a stranger behind a counter
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{est-ce que tu veux un café ?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three singular forms. (\emph{\textbf{Veux, veux, veut}} — all said the same.) You are ordering coffee from someone you have never met: which form do you use? (\emph{\textbf{Je voudrais}}, never \emph{je veux}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pouvoir]{pouvoir — can}

\label{lesson:FR-C33-pouvoir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{je voudrais un café}. That was a want, softened.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pouvoir} — \textbf{to be able}, and in practice \textbf{can}. The singular:

Same chant, three beats:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je peux — tu peux — il peut}
\end{quote}

\emph{I can, you can, he can.} The same pattern you just met: \textbf{all three sound alike}, and the pronoun carries the person. \emph{Peux, peux, peut} — and note it rhymes with nothing in \emph{vouloir}, but behaves identically.

What follows \emph{pouvoir} is a \textbf{plain, unchanged verb}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Je peux parler français.} — I can speak French.
  \item \textbf{Tu peux aider ?} — Can you help?
\end{itemize}

Nothing happens to \emph{parler} or \emph{aider}. They arrive in the dictionary form and stay there, which makes this one of the cheapest structures in French: every verb you already know can be put behind \emph{peux} with no change at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The reason \emph{pouvoir} matters early has little to do with ability.

Asking someone to do something by telling them to do it is abrupt in French, as it is in English. What French reaches for instead is a \textbf{question about ability} — the same move English makes with \emph{can you}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tu peux fermer la porte ?} — Can you close the door?
\end{quote}

Nobody is really asking whether the other person is capable. The question is the politeness, and it is why \emph{pouvoir} buys you more than a translation would suggest. Pair it with the softened form you already know and you get the version for a stranger:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Vous pouvez fermer la porte ?}
\end{quote}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{je peux, tu peux, il peut} — again, one sound between them
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{je peux parler français}
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{tu peux aider ?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to the verb that follows \emph{peux}? (\textbf{Nothing} — it stays in its dictionary form.) Why does a beginner need \emph{pouvoir} early? (Because \textbf{asking whether someone can} is how French makes a polite request.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[devoir]{devoir — must}

\label{lesson:FR-C33-devoir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{je peux parler français}. The second verb did not change.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{devoir} — \textbf{to have to}, \textbf{must}. The singular, and by now you can predict the shape of the problem:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je dois — tu dois — il doit}
\end{quote}

\emph{I must, you must, he must.} \textbf{All three sound alike again.} Three verbs in a row have done this, which is the point worth carrying away: in the French present singular, the three persons are routinely one sound, and the pronoun is what tells them apart. This is not a quirk of these three words.

A plain verb follows, exactly as after \emph{peux}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Je dois partir.} — I must leave.
  \item \textbf{Tu dois attendre.} — You must wait.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{devoir} comes from Latin \emph{\textbf{debere}}, \textbf{to owe} — and it never stopped meaning that. The same French verb still does both jobs:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Je dois partir.} — I must leave.
  \item \textbf{Je te dois dix euros.} — I owe you ten euros.
\end{itemize}

One word, an obligation of time and an obligation of money, because to French they are the same idea: something is owed.

That Latin \emph{debere} is also where English gets \textbf{debt}, \textbf{debit} and \textbf{due} — so a word you have never seen has been sitting in your own vocabulary all along, spelled differently and meaning the half of \emph{devoir} that involves money.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{je dois, tu dois, il doit}
  \item \emph{je dois partir}
  \item \emph{je te dois dix euros} — the same verb, the other meaning
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things does \emph{devoir} mean? (\textbf{Must}, and \textbf{to owe}.) Which English words share its Latin root? (\textbf{Debt}, \textbf{debit}, \textbf{due}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — want, can, must}

\label{lesson:FR-C33-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{je dois partir}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three verbs, one shape between them. Say each chant in turn:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je veux — tu veux — il veut}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je peux — tu peux — il peut}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je dois — tu dois — il doit}
\end{quote}

Every chant is three forms that sound identical, and between the three chants you have wanting, being able, and having to.

And all three do the same structural thing: \textbf{a plain verb follows, unchanged.}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Je veux partir.} — I want to leave.
  \item \textbf{Je peux partir.} — I can leave.
  \item \textbf{Je dois partir.} — I must leave.
\end{itemize}

That is the payoff, and it is larger than three words. Every verb you have learned in this book — \emph{parler}, \emph{aider}, \emph{fermer}, \emph{ouvrir}, \emph{écrire}, \emph{lire}, \emph{dormir} — can be dropped in behind any of these three with \textbf{no change of any kind}. You have not learned three expressions. You have learned three openings, and you already own everything that goes after them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
One caution carried forward, because it is the difference between sounding capable and sounding rude.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Stating a want to a friend: \textbf{je veux}.
  \item Asking anyone for anything: \textbf{je voudrais}.
  \item Asking someone else to act: \textbf{tu peux…?} or \textbf{vous pouvez…?}
\end{itemize}

The blunt form is not wrong French. It is correct French used at the wrong moment, which is a harder mistake to hear and an easier one to make.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{je veux partir, je peux partir, je dois partir}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same three with \emph{parler français} instead of \emph{partir}
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{vous pouvez fermer la porte ?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to a verb placed after \emph{veux}, \emph{peux} or \emph{dois}? (\textbf{Nothing} — it stays in its dictionary form.) You want to ask a stranger to close a window: which of the three do you start with? (\emph{\textbf{Vous pouvez…}})
\end{tcolorbox}
